content.text:
Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for their versatility, giving every client a visual identity pitched at the treatment the task actually calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page — what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in. Format is part of this read — decided, not defaulted: a Markdown publish keeps its filename as its title and takes almost none of the craft below, so it fits only when the user asked for Markdown or the content is bound for a Markdown-native destination; never pick it to save time.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first — CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world — its materials, instruments, vernacular — is where distinctive choices come from. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. The Artifact CSP blocks font CDNs, so don't link a webfont URL and risk a silent fallback. Instead inline the face as a @font-face data URI. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject — the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme, and the viewer has three states, not two: an explicit choice stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting stamps *nothing* — most viewers see the un-stamped document, where only `prefers-color-scheme` separates light from dark. Structure the CSS token-level for all three: the bare `:root` block defines the complete light palette (for a deliberately dark-first design, swap light and dark consistently through this whole pattern); `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` redefines only the tokens, guarded as `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` so an explicit light choice beats a dark OS; `:root[data-theme="dark"]` redefines them again so the toggle also wins in the other direction. Style components through the tokens, never directly inside a media or `[data-theme]` block — a color whose only definition sits behind `[data-theme]` never applies in the un-stamped state, and the page renders one theme's text on the other theme's ground. Two more rules keep each theme resolving as a set: the artifact composites over a ground the viewer paints in *its* theme, so `body` must set an explicit `background` from a token — a transparent body silently borrows the host's ground; and every element that sets a color takes it from the same token set as the surface behind it, never a literal that only works in one theme. Before publishing, scan the stylesheet for any color declared only inside a media or `[data-theme]` block — that is the classic unreadable-artifact bug. Give the second theme the same care as the first — don't naively invert; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both grounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme — then skip the media query and stamps entirely but still paint the background and every color explicitly, so the page holds on either host ground; make it a choice, not an omission.

**Let layout do the spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap`, not per-element margins that silently collapse or double. Wide content — tables, code, diagrams — gets `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. Reach for `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Avoid AI-generated design** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. Where the user pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. Where nothing is specified, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly** Be cognizant of overlapping elements, cascade collisions, silent font fallbacks; visual bugs hide in the gap between source and output. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. For generative or decorative graphics, reach for Canvas or WebGL rather than hand-authoring long SVG path data.

**CSS rules** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificities. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out — a type-based selector like `.section` fighting an element-based one like `.cta` over padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't silently undo your spacing.

**Writing the copy** Words are design material, not decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen — name things by what people recognize, not how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*, not *webhook config*). Active voice; a control says exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it — no apologies, no vagueness. Specific beats clever.

**Name the page like a product, not a caption.** The `<title>` is the artifact's name in the gallery and the browser tab, and it sets the reader's first impression of care. Give the page a real name: a short noun phrase, typically two to four words, specific to the subject — or, for a page that exists to answer one question, that question itself, which is then the page's name. Stop at the name — a title that carries its own explainer after a dash or colon reads as generated filler. The name must also identify the page among many: in the gallery it sits beside dozens of other artifacts, and a generic category label that could sit on any of them fails as a name just as surely as an appended explainer. When a candidate title pairs the name with a generic word — a greeting, a category, a page-type label — the name is the half to keep; a trim that drops the identity and keeps the generic word produces exactly the title that could sit on any page. And the rule removes explainers, it does not impose brevity: a multi-word title that already reads as one specific name is finished, and shortening it further only makes it generic. The one-sentence publish `description` is where the explanation belongs; the gallery shows it right under the title.

**Structure is information** Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

**When it's a UI, not a document** A dashboard or tool is scanned and operated, not read top-to-bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Surface the summary before the detail; encode state in form as well as number — a pill, a chip, a severity stripe — so what needs attention reads at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. What's interactive should look interactive.



## Process

Before writing code, sketch a short design plan — a compact token system with color, type, and layout:
- **Color**: describe the palette as 4–6 named hex values.
- **Type**: typefaces for 2+ roles — a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: a layout concept in one or two sentences.

Then build, following the plan and deriving every color and type decision from it.

## When the request is editorial

The stance shifts: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated calls, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part, and note what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the plan's uniqueness do you write the code, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero is a thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world — headline, image, live demo, interactive moment. 
- Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content. 
- Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, a scroll-triggered reveal, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Spend your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent fights the ground, shift it toward analogous or drop saturation rather than replacing it.
Analysis complete. Writing up Phase 0.

The other six keep a give-up that was designed, not defaulted.

§2 Four findings that change the plan

F1 · blocks full scaffold adoption for 2 durables

jsconsumer.Start is Consume-based and its callbacks are serial

Start calls cons.Consume(onMsg, …), not Fetch. For the nine serial consumers that is fine — MaxMessages: 1 (or KeepInProgress, which forces it) reproduces today's Fetch(1) pacing and keeps NumPending honest for KEDA. For cmd/fanout's two pooled consumers (FANOUT_DISPATCH_CONCURRENCY=8 in every cell) it does not: hosting the pool under a serial callback moves the FetchBatch ≤ Concurrency AckWait bound onto MaxMessages, and Runner.Stop discards the prefetch buffer where the engine today drains every fetched message to its disposition. Discarded prefetch means redelivery on another pod, which misses the in-process route memo and re-publishes every route — and mirror_git_v1's dedup window is 1s, so those are real duplicate git syncs.

This is the same wall entire-search hit on trail #131: it declined jsconsumer.Start to keep its 16-worker pool and its ENT-1460 drain, and adopted Retry + Schedule only. Proposal: follow that precedent for both cmd/fanout consumers — keep the fetch loop and pool, adopt the server ladder, Retry and Schedule validation. Consequence to record: COR-1254's “0 hand-rolled fetch loops” exit criterion is not reachable for cmd/fanout without a go-nuts follow-up (Runner.Drain + a pool-friendly consume), which trail #131 already logged as needed.

F2 · rules out a server ladder for the worker

A BackOff ladder would collapse the worker's 15-minute ack budget

Two mechanisms interlock. First, the server normalizes stored AckWait to BackOff[0], and Schedule.Validate rejects any disagreement — so giving the worker a ladder forces ackWait = backoff[0]. Second, natsmsg.KeepInProgress caps extension at 15 ticks of AckWait/3 ≈ 5×AckWait. At today's AckWait 15m the cap is 75m, comfortably above the 30m defaultSyncTimeout. With a 30s first rung the cap becomes 2m30s — every multi-GB clone would be redelivered mid-run to a second replica, manufacturing exactly the concurrent-sync races the ErrTargetRefMoved path exists to absorb.

Doing nothing instead (no ladder, no client delay) is worse still: redelivery falls back to AckWait, so the flat 30s cadence becomes 15m × 9 = 2h15m, against a 6h stream maxAge on a work-queue that discards regardless of ack state. The worker therefore keeps a client-scheduled flat NakWithDelay(30s) as its sole scheduler — no server BackOff, so this is not mixed ownership and Schedule validates it clean. It is nonetheless a conscious deviation from the 2026-08-12 “server owns the ladder” decision and needs your sign-off (§5).

F3 · changes what the advisory backstops watch

Capture-then-Ack makes MSG_TERMINATED stop firing

webhook-forwarder and cmd/fanout each run an in-process pod-crash backstop subscribed to MAX_DELIVERIES and MSG_TERMINATED on their own durable, to re-capture a delivery lost between “give up” and “publish to the DLQ”. Under Retry the consumer Acks rather than Terms, and dead-letters at MaxDeliver − CaptureReserve rather than exhausting — so both advisories go quiet on the normal path. That gap is filled better by the reserve delivery (a failed capture is retried rather than dropped), but the backstop's remaining job shrinks to the stranded case and the operator guidance must say so. Same class of doc drift the #131 review found in the ack-floor monitor.

F4 · mandatory pre-flight on every migration PR

Start always sends AckWait, MaxDeliver, InactiveThreshold, MaxAckPending and BackOff. Two consequences. The good one: InactiveThreshold is applied natively, so the ensureInactiveThreshold read-modify-write hack in forwarder.go and engine.go — which exists only because legacy PullSubscribe binds and silently ignores the field — is deleted, not ported. The dangerous one: a zero MaxAckPending resets a live durable to the server default of 1000, and any immutable-field disagreement (AckPolicy, DeliverPolicy, ReplayPolicy, MaxWaiting) fails loudly and non-retryably, which Run returns and main treats as fatal — a crash-loop on rollout.

So every migration PR opens with nats consumer info -j <stream> <durable> against staging and prod, and its trail body carries the diff between the stored config and the config jsconsumer will render. Anything not intended to change is set explicitly.

That is exactly the failure a config-changing migration PR could introduce and not see. I have not reproduced the canary's specific defect — it stays a separate triage item, and the backfill flips get an explicit “consumer actually subscribed” check in their verification plan rather than trusting /readyz.

§4 Migration order

Ordered by blast radius and by whether give-up semantics move. Every branch bases on main (or on PR-0 once merged), never on a sibling. Numbering here is a real sequence — each step's staging soak is the gate on the next.

  1. PR-0 — shared plumbinggo-nuts v0.9.1-0.20260811… → 832d765 + re-vendor (the vendored copy has no jsconsumer at all); embedded nats-server test harness; a shared Schedule conformance test. No consumer touched, no durable written. Verdict in §5.

  3. webhook-forwarderThe only loop where the full Retry model is unambiguously right and its DLQ and grant are already live. US-only. Proves capture-then-Ack in production before any engine consumer needs it.
  4. fanoutengine runtime switchIntroduces the jsconsumer-backed path, default off. Zero durables change; this PR is reviewable as pure structure.
  5. meta-fanout-backfill-prs, then meta-fanout-backfillIdle work-queues, no live-path coupling, give-up preserved. The cheapest possible first flips of the engine switch.
  6. trails-fanout-push, then trails-fanout-pull-requestSerial, lowest-traffic webhooks_github_v1 consumers with a working DLQ. First engine consumers to take Retry.
  7. core-fanoutSerial, Retry, and the one adopter with an external timing constraint (the 5m push-author dedup window) — worth its own staging window.
  8. meta-fanout (live webhook)Serial, give-up unchanged. Later than its siblings only because a stall here is visible to display metadata across every cell.
  9. native-mirror-fanoutFirst pooled consumer, on a limits stream where a dropped event self-heals on the next push — the safe place to prove the pooled shape.
  10. fanout-<region>Pooled, 8 workers, highest traffic, publishes the git-sync jobs everything downstream depends on. Last of the engine.
  11. cmd/workerLast. Most bespoke machinery — heartbeat, KV fail-index, advisory backstop, publish-before-ack ordering, KEDA on every cell — and the only loop whose ladder decision deviates from the program default.
  12. Cleanup — delete the engine switchRemoves the legacy fetch path and the dual runtime once all eight have soaked.

§5 PR-0: needed

Yes — and it is the difference between twelve independent PRs and twelve PRs that each carry the same three unrelated changes.

  • go-nuts bump + re-vendor. mirror-pipeline pins v0.9.1-0.20260811083507-143ec67e8cfa, two days before trail #13 merged; the vendored tree has no jsconsumer package. Without this, PR #2 owns a dependency bump that every later PR conflicts with.
  • Embedded nats-server harness. mirror-pipeline has zero broker-level tests today — interface fakes only, as COR-1009 records. nats-server/v2 is not currently a dependency, so adding it drags a large vendor tree; that cost belongs in one PR, not five. Modelled on go-nuts internal/brokersemantics (startServer / connect, pinned server version).
  • Shared Schedule conformance test. One helper that asserts a consumer's declared timing contract via the exported jsconsumer.Schedule, so every later PR proves its ladder rather than restating arithmetic — including the two loops (worker, lifecycle) whose configs Start would not otherwise validate.

Nothing else. No consumer, no durable, no fleet file. PR-0 is a green build and a new test that passes.

§6 Decisions I need before writing code

1 · The worker keeps a client-side ladder

F2 shows a server BackOff is mechanically unavailable to the worker and “do nothing” is worse than either alternative. That makes cmd/worker a standing exception to the 2026-08-12 ladder-ownership decision. I'd document it in the trail and on COR-1254 rather than quietly ship it. Confirm the exception, or tell me to take the 2h15m AckWait-driven ladder instead.

2 · cmd/fanout does not adopt the scaffold

Its two pooled consumers take the ladder, Retry and Schedule but keep their fetch loop, per the entire-search precedent. This leaves COR-1254's “0 hand-rolled fetch loops” unmet for one binary pending a go-nuts follow-up. Accept, or hold both cmd/fanout consumers until go-nuts grows Runner.Drain and a pool-friendly consume?

3 · Engine switch, or one engine PR

A per-consumer switch costs a temporary dual path but is what makes eight durables independently mergeable, revertable, and stage-watchable. One engine PR is cleaner code and moves all eight in staging at once. I recommend the switch; confirm.

4 · Three smaller calls

(a) webhook-forwarder shape A (maxDeliver 9, envelope preserved) over B (maxDeliver 8, one attempt lost) — I recommend A. (b) The panic path keeps its no-capture stance under Retry. (c) The trails-fanout 24h vs 72h InactiveThreshold divergence: leave it and document, or normalize in a separate fleet-free PR.

Not touched, by rule: no grant is widened in place. The four gaps found — a mirror_git DLQ + mirror-worker grant, a resource_lifecycle DLQ + meta-fanout grant, a repo.refs.dlq.v1.> grant for fanout, and a webhooks.github.dlq.> grant for meta-fanout — are recorded here as fleet changes and left out of every migration PR.

**Phase 0 done — analysis only, no code.** Full write-up: https://claude.ai/code/artifact/f1ac585e-924c-446f-aa87-87fe9a3a8798

Read: COR-1254 (all three comments incl. the canary verdict + park decision), COR-1252 program status, ENT-1601's A1-merged comment (plus the surrounding decision thread), COR-1009. Also pulled entire-search trail #131 — it changed two conclusions below.

### The headline

**The four loops are eleven durables.** `pkg/fanoutengine` is one runtime shared by four binaries and eight consumers, each with its own durable and KEDA scaler. "One trail per consumer" means ~12 PRs.

**Scaffold migrates everywhere; give-up changes in five of eleven** — exactly the set where a DLQ stream *and* a matching publish grant already exist and are enabled: `webhook-forwarder`, `fanout-<region>`, `core-fanout`, `trails-fanout-push`, `trails-fanout-pull-request`. The other six keep a designed give-up (worker's KV fail-index + rekick, the two backfills' `TermOnExhaustion`, lifecycle and native-mirror's drop-at-exhaustion on retaining streams).

**InactiveThreshold**: reliance is concentrated in the six `webhooks_github_v1` durables (72h, except trails-fanout at 24h). All preserved — and *improved*: `jsconsumer.Start` sends it on `CreateOrUpdateConsumer`, so the `ensureInactiveThreshold` read-modify-write hack gets deleted rather than ported. The five durables with no threshold are all on workqueue/limits streams where it's correctly absent; recorded explicitly per loop rather than left implicit.

### Four findings that changed the plan

1. **`jsconsumer.Start` is `Consume`-based, callbacks serial.** Fine for the nine serial consumers (`MaxMessages: 1` reproduces `Fetch(1)` pacing, KEDA `NumPending` stays honest). Not fine for `cmd/fanout`'s two pooled consumers (concurrency 8 in every cell): `Runner.Stop` discards the prefetch buffer where the engine today drains it, and a discarded message redelivers to a pod that misses the route memo → duplicate git syncs (`mirror_git_v1` dedup window is 1s). This is the exact wall #131 hit. Proposal: same precedent — ladder + `Retry` + `Schedule` only, keep the fetch loop.

## Conclusion: yes — migrate, but not uniformly

Nothing in mirror-pipeline blocks adoption. The library fits, the durables can be updated in place (no recreation, no redelivery storms), and **no fleet change is required for the migration itself**. But "migrate to go-nuts" resolves into three different depths, and pretending it's one thing is how this goes wrong:

| Depth | Durables | What they take |
|---|---|---|
| Full scaffold | 9 of 11 | `Run`/`Process`, server ladder, lifecycle, shutdown |
| Partial (`Retry` + `Schedule` only) | 2 — `cmd/fanout`'s pooled consumers | ladder + capture, keep their own fetch loop |
| `Retry`/capture-then-Ack give-up | 5 of 11 | only where a DLQ *and* grant already exist and are on |

The other six keep the give-up they were designed with — the worker's KV fail-index + rekick, the two backfills' `TermOnExhaustion`, lifecycle/native-mirror's drop-onto-a-retaining-stream. Those aren't gaps to close; converting them would need four new grants and two new DLQ streams to buy nothing.

## Why it's worth doing

Concretely, not abstractly: it deletes the `ensureInactiveThreshold` read-modify-write hack in two places (the library applies the 2026-06-01 safety valve natively), replaces the worker's uncapped heartbeat with a capped one that restores the broker's liveness failsafe, gives every loop a validated timing contract instead of arithmetic in comments, and puts eleven consumers on the path where library fixes land once. The 48h-backlog failure class — an app config silently overriding AckWait — becomes a startup error.

## The one honest asterisk

`cmd/fanout` can't take the scaffold today. `Start`'s `Consume` callbacks are serial and `Runner.Stop` discards prefetch, which would turn every rollout into duplicate git syncs through the route memo. entire-search hit the identical wall on #131 and took the same partial path. So **COR-1254's "0 hand-rolled fetch loops" exit criterion is not reachable for one binary** until go-nuts grows `Runner.Drain` + a pool-friendly consume — a follow-up #131 already logged. I'd rather ship ten migrations and say that plainly than force the eleventh and eat duplicate syncs.

## Recommendation

Approve PR-0 and the first two loops (lifecycle, then webhook-forwarder). Those two prove the whole model — scaffold + server ladder on one, capture-then-Ack on the other — across staging with nothing else moving, and if either soaks badly you've spent two small PRs, not a program.

What I need before touching code: **the worker's client-ladder exception** (mechanically forced, but it deviates from a decision you recorded), and **the engine switch vs one engine PR** call. The other two asks can ride in their own PRs.

What would change my answer: if a live `nats consumer info -j` snapshot shows the durables carrying config the legacy client never declared — a non-default `MaxAckPending`, an unexpected `MaxWaiting` — the first `CreateOrUpdateConsumer` becomes a config change rather than a no-op. Track D phase-0 read-out. Sources: mirror-pipeline ba09d45, go-nuts 832d765, fleet bd4d9a8fa, plus entire-search trail #131 (which changed two of my conclusions). Full write-up with the timing tables: https://claude.ai/code/artifact/f1ac585e-924c-446f-aa87-87fe9a3a8798

=== LEAD: NOT-FULLY-MIGRATABLE + FLEET-SIDE ===

Nothing needs a fleet change BEFORE migration. Zero grants widened, zero streams added, no durable recreated. The migration is app-side only.

ONE partial: cmd/fanout's two POOLED consumers (fanout-<region>, native-mirror-fanout; FANOUT_DISPATCH_CONCURRENCY=8 in every cell) cannot take the jsconsumer scaffold. jsconsumer.Start uses cons.Consume() with serial callbacks, and Runner.Stop discards the prefetch buffer where the engine today explicitly drains every fetched message to its disposition. A discarded prefetch redelivers to another pod, which misses the in-process route memo and re-publishes every route — and mirror_git_v1's dedup window is 1s, so those are REAL duplicate git syncs. entire-search hit the identical wall on #131 and took Retry+Schedule only, keeping its 16-worker pool. I propose the same. Consequence: COR-1254's "0 hand-rolled fetch loops" exit criterion is unreachable for one binary until go-nuts grows Runner.Drain + a pool-friendly consume — a follow-up #131 already logged.

FOUR grant/DLQ gaps found, recorded, deliberately NOT actioned (no in-place widening): mirror_git DLQ + mirror-worker grant; resource_lifecycle DLQ + meta-fanout grant; repo.refs.dlq.v1.> grant for fanout; webhooks.github.dlq.> grant for meta-fanout. Each would be a fleet change to enable capture on a loop that today has a working non-DLQ give-up. None are prerequisites.

=== PER-LOOP TABLE (4 loops = 11 durables) ===

The four loops in the brief resolve to eleven durables, because pkg/fanoutengine is ONE runtime shared by four binaries and eight consumers, each with its own durable and KEDA scaler. "One trail per consumer" therefore means ~12 PRs, not four.

Legend: SCAFFOLD = jsconsumer.Run/Process only, give-up unchanged. SCAFFOLD+RETRY = plus capture-then-Ack to a DLQ. PARTIAL = Retry+Schedule, keeps own fetch loop.

--- Loop 1: cmd/worker (hand-rolled) ---
durable mirror-git-v1-<jur>-<cluster> | mirror_git_v1 | workqueue, maxAge 6h | all cells | KEDA
  now: client NakWithDelay 30s x9, ackWait 15m, maxDeliver 10, no server BackOff; uncapped InProgress heartbeat at 5m; syncTimeout 30m
  give-up: Term + failindex.RecordFailure (KV) + failed mirror_done completion; rekicker CronJob replays. Plus a MAX_DELIVERIES/MSG_TERMINATED advisory backstop for the pod-crash gap.
  InactiveThreshold: NONE, and correct — workqueue pins nothing when a durable idles. Recorded explicitly as 0 with that reason, not left implicit.
  DLQ: none, no grant.
  target: SCAFFOLD. KeepInProgress:true (forces MaxMessages 1, preserving Fetch(1) pacing and honest NumPending for KEDA). Give-up UNCHANGED — the KV fail-index + rekick is a designed give-up path, not an absent one; converting it to Retry would need a new stream + a new grant to buy strictly less (the rekicker re-drives the job; a DLQ would only store it).
  Ladder: keeps client NakWithDelay(30s) as SOLE scheduler — see contradiction #2 below. Not mixed ownership (no server BackOff), and Schedule{NakDelay:30s, MaxDeliver:10, AckWait:15m, StreamMaxAge:6h}.Validate() == [].

--- Loop 2: cmd/webhook-forwarder (hand-rolled) ---
durable webhook-forwarder | webhooks_github_v1 | interest, maxAge 96h | US only
  now: Nak 30s x7, ackWait 30s, maxDeliver 8
  give-up: DLQ capture then Term on bad envelope / 401-403 / other 4xx / exhaustion. Panic path deliberately Naks with NO capture even on the final delivery.
  InactiveThreshold: 72h, LOAD-BEARING (2026-06-01 interest-stream valve, sized under the 96h maxAge). Preserved.
  DLQ: webhooks_github_dlq present, grant "webhooks.github.dlq.>" present, ENTIRE_WEBHOOK_DLQ_ENABLED=true in both cells.
  target: SCAFFOLD+RETRY. The one loop where capture-then-Ack is unambiguously right: dead-lettering is ALREADY the designed outcome and all three preconditions are live. Server ladder, disposition becomes do-nothing, ackWait = backOff[0] = 30s.
  Shape A (recommended): maxDeliver 9, len(backOff) 8 x 30s, Retry maxDeliver 9, captureReserve 1 -> dead-letter at delivery 8 = 3m30s, reserve at 4m00s. Preserves today's 8 handler attempts and 3m30s envelope byte-for-byte. Shape B (maxDeliver 8 + reserve 1) costs one attempt and shortens to 3m00s.

--- Loop 3: cmd/meta-fanout lifecycle (hand-rolled) ---
durable meta-fanout-lifecycle | resource_lifecycle_v1 | limits, maxAge 96h (staging overlays trim to 6h) | all cells
  now: Nak 30s x7, ackWait 30s, maxDeliver 8. No Term path at all — verbatim cross-region republish, nothing can be permanently unprocessable.
  give-up: silent drop at MaxDeliver; the source stream retains the event for its full maxAge, so replay is a separate already-documented path.
  InactiveThreshold: NONE, correct — limits retention, an idle durable pins nothing.
  DLQ: none, no grant.
  target: SCAFFOLD. Give-up unchanged: a DLQ here would duplicate retention that already exists. Server ladder flat 30s x7, ackWait 30s, maxDeliver 8, disposition do-nothing. No Retry, so no capture reserve and no third MaxDeliver to reconcile.

--- Loop 4: pkg/fanoutengine (8 consumers, 4 binaries) ---
All eight today: Nak 30s x7, ackWait 30s, maxDeliver 8 (3m30s to give-up).
  a) fanout-<region> | webhooks_github_v1 interest | US | POOLED 8 | IT 72h load-bearing | DLQ+grant+enabled YES -> PARTIAL+Retry
  b) native-mirror-fanout | repo_refs_v1 limits | all cells | POOLED 8 | IT none (correct, limits) | repo_refs_dlq_v1 EXISTS but fanout has NO repo.refs.dlq.v1.> grant; no DLQ wired by design ("next push re-heals" is the accepted RPO) -> PARTIAL, give-up unchanged
  c) core-fanout | webhooks_github_v1 | US | serial | IT 72h | DLQ+grant (narrow: ...dlq.core-fanout) -> SCAFFOLD+RETRY. Binding constraint: total redelivery span must stay under github_push_author_v1's 5m dedup window; 3m30s preserved with room.
  d) meta-fanout (live webhook) | webhooks_github_v1 | US | serial | IT 72h | NO DLQ, NO grant (deliberate, documented in the fleet manifest) -> SCAFFOLD, give-up unchanged
  e) trails-fanout-push | webhooks_github_v1 | US | serial | IT 24h | DLQ+grant -> SCAFFOLD+RETRY
  f) trails-fanout-pull-request | same as (e) -> SCAFFOLD+RETRY
  g) meta-fanout-backfill | github_meta_backfill workqueue, maxAge 720h | US | serial | IT none (correct — idle between runs is normal) | no DLQ -> SCAFFOLD, give-up unchanged (TermOnExhaustion is the designed work-queue drain, COR-762)
  h) meta-fanout-backfill-prs | github_pr_backfill, same shape -> SCAFFOLD, give-up unchanged

Summary: scaffold everywhere (9 full + 2 partial); Retry/DLQ in 5 of 11 — exactly the set where a DLQ stream AND a matching publish grant already exist and are enabled. The other 6 keep a give-up that was designed, not defaulted.

=== MIGRATION ORDER (lowest risk first) ===
Every branch bases on main (or PR-0 once merged), never on a sibling. Rationale in brackets.
0. PR-0 shared plumbing [see below]
1. meta-fanout-lifecycle [smallest hand-rolled loop, limits stream, low volume, give-up unchanged — proves scaffold + server ladder with nothing else moving]
2. webhook-forwarder [only loop where full Retry is unambiguously right and all three preconditions are already live; US-only — proves capture-then-Ack in prod before any engine consumer needs it]
3. fanoutengine runtime switch, default OFF [zero durables change; reviewable as pure structure]
4. meta-fanout-backfill-prs, then meta-fanout-backfill [idle work-queues, no live-path coupling, give-up preserved — cheapest first flips]
5. trails-fanout-push, then -pull-request [serial, lowest-traffic webhooks_github_v1 consumers with a working DLQ; first engine consumers to take Retry]
6. core-fanout [serial + Retry + the only external timing constraint (5m dedup window) — earns its own staging window]
7. meta-fanout live [serial, give-up unchanged; later than siblings only because a stall is visible to display metadata in every cell]
8. native-mirror-fanout [first pooled consumer, on a limits stream where a dropped event self-heals on the next push — safe place to prove the pooled shape]
9. fanout-<region> [pooled, 8 workers, highest traffic, publishes the git-sync jobs everything downstream depends on — last of the engine]
10. cmd/worker [last: most bespoke machinery — heartbeat, KV fail-index, advisory backstop, publish-before-ack ordering, KEDA in every cell — and the only ladder decision that deviates from the program default]
11. cleanup: delete the engine switch + legacy fetch path

Note on the switch (step 3): staging auto-promotes on every push to main, so a single engine PR would move all eight durables in staging simultaneously. The per-consumer switch is what preserves Andrea's "watch staging between merges" cadence. It is temporary scaffolding with a named deletion PR.

=== PR-0: NEEDED ===
Three things every later PR would otherwise duplicate or conflict on:
1. go-nuts bump + re-vendor. mirror-pipeline pins v0.9.1-0.20260811083507-143ec67e8cfa — two days BEFORE trail #13 merged — and the vendored tree has no jsconsumer package at all.
2. Embedded nats-server harness. mirror-pipeline has ZERO broker-level tests today (interface fakes only, as COR-1009 records), and nats-server/v2 is not currently a dependency, so adding it drags a large vendor tree. That cost belongs in one PR, not five. Modelled on go-nuts internal/brokersemantics (startServer/connect, pinned server version).
3. A shared Schedule conformance helper, so every later PR proves its ladder via the exported jsconsumer.Schedule rather than restating arithmetic — including the two loops (worker, lifecycle) whose configs Start would not otherwise validate.
Nothing else. No consumer, no durable, no fleet file.

=== SURPRISES / CONTRADICTIONS WITH THE RECORD ===

1. CONTRADICTS COR-1254 exit criterion. "0 hand-rolled fetch loops" is unreachable for cmd/fanout without a go-nuts change (see LEAD). The canary's sequencing conclusion — library first, CRs second — still holds; this is a further qualification on the library half.

2. CONTRADICTS the recorded ladder-ownership decision (COR-1254 2026-08-12, "migrating apps drop any client-side redelivery scheduling"). cmd/worker mechanically cannot. Two interlocking facts: (a) the server normalizes stored AckWait to BackOff[0] and Schedule.Validate rejects any disagreement, so a ladder forces ackWait = backoff[0]; (b) natsmsg.KeepInProgress caps extension at 15 ticks of AckWait/3 ~= 5x AckWait. At today's 15m that cap is 75m, comfortably above the 30m defaultSyncTimeout. At a 30s first rung it becomes 2m30s — every multi-GB clone would be redelivered mid-run to a second replica, manufacturing exactly the concurrent-sync races ErrTargetRefMoved exists to absorb. Doing nothing instead is worse: redelivery falls back to AckWait, so 30s flat becomes 15m x 9 = 2h15m against a 6h workqueue maxAge that discards regardless of ack state. So the worker keeps a client-scheduled flat Nak as its sole scheduler. This needs Andrea's explicit sign-off as a standing exception.

3. QUALIFIES the canary's InactiveThreshold finding. The canary comment says "every fanout loop relies on server-side InactiveThreshold reaping". Measured: only 6 of 11 durables carry one — the four webhooks_github_v1 fanouts plus webhook-forwarder (72h) and the two trails-fanout durables (24h). The worker, lifecycle, both backfills and native-mirror-fanout have NONE, correctly, because they sit on workqueue/limits streams where an idle durable pins nothing. The reliance is real but narrower than recorded, and it is confined to one stream.

4. The library migration IMPROVES the InactiveThreshold story rather than threatening it. jsconsumer.Start sends InactiveThreshold on CreateOrUpdateConsumer, so the ensureInactiveThreshold read-modify-write hack — which exists in forwarder.go and engine.go only because legacy PullSubscribe binds to an existing consumer and silently ignores the field — gets DELETED, not ported. Relevant to CR reactivation precondition #2 on COR-1254: the migration does not resolve the "a CR permanently defeats reaping" problem, but it does move the app half onto a declarative field, which is the surface a redesign would build on.

5. UNRECORDED HAZARD: CreateOrUpdateConsumer writes fields the legacy client never sent. A zero MaxAckPending resets a live durable to the server default 1000, and any immutable-field disagreement (AckPolicy, DeliverPolicy, ReplayPolicy, MaxWaiting) fails loudly and NON-retryably — Run returns it and main treats it as fatal, i.e. a crash-loop on rollout. Mitigation, per-PR not program-level: open every migration PR with `nats consumer info -j <stream> <durable>` against staging AND prod, and carry the stored-vs-rendered diff in the trail body. This is the one part of my analysis reasoned from code rather than measured against live config.

6. UNRECORDED SIDE EFFECT of capture-then-Ack: the MAX_DELIVERIES / MSG_TERMINATED advisory backstops in webhook-forwarder and cmd/fanout go quiet on the normal give-up path, because the consumer Acks rather than Terms and dead-letters at MaxDeliver-CaptureReserve rather than exhausting. The reserve delivery replaces them (a failed capture is retried rather than dropped), which is better — but the backstop's remaining job shrinks to the stranded case and the operator guidance must say so. Same class of doc drift the #131 review found in the ack-floor monitor.

7. A number worth knowing: the worker's worst-case wall clock to give-up is ~5h04m (10 attempts x 30m sync budget + a 4m30s ladder) against mirror_git_v1's 6h maxAge. Schedule.Validate passes because it counts SCHEDULED waits only (4m30s) — handler time sits on top, as the library documents. Not a defect, but the margin is thinner than anything on the record suggests.

8. One genuinely bare Term survives in the worker (consumer.go:231, malformed-subject reject) — it records nothing because it has no target ULID to key on. Closing it needs a mirror_git DLQ + a mirror-worker grant. Flagged, not bundled.

9. Carried forward UNREPRODUCED: the canary's meta-fanout-backfill /readyz finding. What I can confirm from the code is that readinessGate deliberately excludes both backfill consumers, so a backfill durable that cannot subscribe leaves the pod Ready while draining nothing — exactly the failure a config-changing migration PR could introduce and not see. I did not reproduce the canary's specific defect; it stays a separate triage item, and the backfill flips get an explicit "consumer actually subscribed" check rather than trusting /readyz.

=== NET RECOMMENDATION ===
Migrate. Approve PR-0 plus loops 1 and 2 (lifecycle, webhook-forwarder) — those two prove the whole model (scaffold + server ladder on one, capture-then-Ack on the other) across staging with nothing else moving; if either soaks badly the cost is two small PRs, not a program. Blocking decisions for Andrea: (i) confirm the worker's client-ladder exception, (ii) accept the cmd/fanout partial adoption (or hold both its consumers for the go-nuts follow-up), (iii) engine switch vs one engine PR. Three smaller calls can ride in their own PRs: forwarder shape A vs B, whether the panic path keeps its no-capture stance under Retry, and the trails-fanout 24h vs 72h InactiveThreshold divergence (looks like drift rather than intent — worth a line of rationale or a normalization, but not silently inside a migration PR).

## mise-tasks/dev/_default
#!/usr/bin/env bash
#MISE description="Start webhook-ingest, fanout, and worker against local NATS + entiredb"
#MISE depends=["dev:streams"]
#USAGE flag "--ingest_port <ingest_port>" help="HTTP port for cmd/webhook-ingest (default 9080)"
#USAGE flag "--fanout_port <fanout_port>" help="HTTP port for cmd/fanout (default 9082)"
#USAGE flag "--worker_port <worker_port>" help="HTTP port for cmd/worker (default 9081)"

set -eu
set -o monitor # Run jobs in their own process group so that we can kill them in cleanup

INGEST_PORT="${usage_ingest_port:-9080}"
FANOUT_PORT="${usage_fanout_port:-9082}"
WORKER_PORT="${usage_worker_port:-9081}"

# Track PIDs
INGEST_PID=""
FANOUT_PID=""
WORKER_PID=""
SHUTTING_DOWN=0

# shellcheck disable=SC2329 # Invoked by the signal/EXIT trap below.
cleanup() {
  if [ "$SHUTTING_DOWN" -eq 1 ]; then
    return
  fi
  SHUTTING_DOWN=1
  echo ""
  echo "Shutting down services..."

  if [ -n "$INGEST_PID" ]; then
    echo "Shutting down webhook-ingest..."
    kill -INT "$INGEST_PID" 2>/dev/null || true
  fi

  if [ -n "$FANOUT_PID" ]; then
    echo "Shutting down fanout..."
    kill -INT "$FANOUT_PID" 2>/dev/null || true
  fi

  if [ -n "$WORKER_PID" ]; then
    echo "Shutting down worker..."
    kill -INT "$WORKER_PID" 2>/dev/null || true
  fi
}

trap cleanup INT TERM EXIT

# Config comes from .env (auto-loaded via mise.toml's `[env] _.file = ".env"`).
# Run `mise run dev:secrets` once to generate .env from .env.example.
if [ ! -f .env ]; then
  echo "WARN: .env not found — run 'mise run dev:secrets' to populate it from 1Password."
fi

mkdir -p ./bin

echo "Building webhook-ingest..."
go build -o ./bin/webhook-ingest ./cmd/webhook-ingest/

echo "Building fanout..."
go build -o ./bin/fanout ./cmd/fanout/

echo "Building worker..."
go build -o ./bin/worker ./cmd/worker/

echo "Starting webhook-ingest on :$INGEST_PORT..."
# webhook-ingest no longer talks to entire-core — it just publishes raw
# webhooks to NATS. No internal-TLS certs needed here after the cmd/fanout
# split.
LISTEN_ADDR=":$INGEST_PORT" \
  ./bin/webhook-ingest &
INGEST_PID=$!

# webhook-ingest owns the webhooks_github_v1 stream; fanout subscribes to it
# and ensures mirror_git_v1 / mirror_perms_v1. Wait for /readyz (NATS
# connected + webhooks stream ensured) before launching fanout so the
# subscribe doesn't bounce on ErrStreamNotFound.
echo "Waiting for webhook-ingest /readyz..."
for i in $(seq 1 50); do
  if ! kill -0 "$INGEST_PID" 2>/dev/null; then
    echo "ERROR: webhook-ingest exited before becoming ready."
    exit 1
  fi
  if curl -fsS "http://localhost:$INGEST_PORT/readyz" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    break
  fi
  if [ "$i" -eq 50 ]; then
    echo "ERROR: webhook-ingest did not become ready within 10s."
    exit 1
  fi
  sleep 0.2
done

echo "Starting fanout on :$FANOUT_PORT..."
# Fanout talks to entire-core's internal RPC for repo placement lookups.
# RepoLookup is gated by AllowWorkloads(WorkloadWebhookIngest), so we keep
# presenting the webhook-ingest SPIFFE identity for now — adding a dedicated
# fanout workload identity is a follow-up.
LISTEN_ADDR=":$FANOUT_PORT" \
  ENTIRE_INTERNAL_TLS_CERT_FILE="../entiredb/certs/internal-cert-webhook-ingest.pem" \
  ENTIRE_INTERNAL_TLS_KEY_FILE="../entiredb/certs/internal-key-webhook-ingest.pem" \
  FANOUT_DURABLE="fanout-dev" \
  ./bin/fanout &
FANOUT_PID=$!

# cmd/worker is a strict consumer and exits immediately if mirror_git_v1
# isn't present. Wait for fanout's /readyz before launching the worker.
echo "Waiting for fanout /readyz..."
for i in $(seq 1 50); do
  if ! kill -0 "$FANOUT_PID" 2>/dev/null; then
    echo "ERROR: fanout exited before becoming ready."
    exit 1
  fi
  if curl -fsS "http://localhost:$FANOUT_PORT/readyz" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    break
  fi
  if [ "$i" -eq 50 ]; then
    echo "ERROR: fanout did not become ready within 10s."
    exit 1
  fi
  sleep 0.2
done

echo "Starting worker on :$WORKER_PORT..."
LISTEN_ADDR=":$WORKER_PORT" ./bin/worker &
WORKER_PID=$!

# Fail the whole task if any service exits. A bare `wait` keeps waiting for the
# two survivors, which made a dead worker look like a healthy local pipeline.
while sleep 1; do
  if [ "$SHUTTING_DOWN" -eq 1 ]; then
    exit 0
  fi
  if ! kill -0 "$INGEST_PID" 2>/dev/null; then
    echo "ERROR: webhook-ingest exited unexpectedly." >&2
    exit 1
  fi
  if ! kill -0 "$FANOUT_PID" 2>/dev/null; then
    echo "ERROR: fanout exited unexpectedly." >&2
    exit 1
  fi
  if ! kill -0 "$WORKER_PID" 2>/dev/null; then
    echo "ERROR: worker exited unexpectedly." >&2
    exit 1
  fi
done

exit 0

chore(deps): go-nuts 832d765 + the broker harness and timing-contract helper (COR-1254)

PR-0 of Track D: shared plumbing only. No consumer, no durable, no fleet
file. Every later loop PR bases on this, so each one carries a migration
and nothing else.

Three parts.

1. go-nuts v0.9.1-0.20260811083507 -> v0.9.1-0.20260813130528-832d765dac1b.
   The old pin predates trail #13 by two days, so the vendored tree had no
   jsconsumer package at all and natsmsg was missing KeepInProgress's tick
   cap and the DLQ publisher's header policy. Nothing in this repo imports
   jsconsumer yet; it vendors here because internal/timingcontract below
   does.

2. internal/natstest — an embedded JetStream nats-server for tests.
   mirror-pipeline has had zero broker-level coverage: every consume-loop
   test drives interface fakes that encode the same model as the code, so
   they agree with it exactly when it is wrong. That is the gap COR-1009
   names as a gate for the loop ports, and the one go-nuts closed for
   itself with internal/brokersemantics after every A1 P1 turned out to be
   a model error rather than a coding one.

   It exposes BOTH handles on one broker — LegacyJetStream for the loops as
   they are today, JetStream for a migrated one — so a migration can be
   measured rather than asserted: characterise the legacy loop, then show
   the new one reproduces it. Two assertions written against two different
   fakes would not be evidence of anything.

   Three tests ship with it. TestVersionAttribution keeps failures
   attributable to a server version. REDACTED
   measures the fact cmd/worker's client-ladder exception rests on: a
   durable given a BackOff ladder does not keep its requested AckWait, the
   server stores BackOff[0] in its place, so "own the ladder server-side"
   and "keep this AckWait" are one knob rather than two. Growing rungs on
   purpose — on a flat ladder that assertion passes whether the
   normalization happens or not. TestNoProductionImport keeps the embedded
   server out of shipped binaries, and guards itself against passing
   vacuously by pinning that the walk reached a known consume loop.

3. internal/timingcontract — a consumer's redelivery timing as data,
   checked by go-nuts' exported jsconsumer.Schedule rather than by hand,
   plus the renderer for the before/after table every migration trail
   carries. ENT-1535 was a consumer whose real envelope was 34h22m against
   a config advertising 17h45m; duplicated timing arithmetic is how that
   happens, so nothing is restated here. Two of this repo's loops
   (cmd/worker, the meta-fanout lifecycle fan) carry neither a server
   ladder nor a Retry, so jsconsumer.Start's own schedule check never runs
   for them — which is exactly why it has to be reachable from a test.

   Pure by construction: no testing import, no NATS connection, no clock,
   so it carries none of natstest's production-import hazard.

Two judgment calls worth a reviewer's attention.

nats-server is pinned to 2.14.4, not the 2.14.3 go-nuts resolves. The
harness exists to attribute semantics to the server that actually runs,
and fleet runs 2.14.4 (apps/nats/base/helmrelease.yaml). It is a test-only
dependency, so this does not reach any shipped binary — but it does pull
x/sys, x/text and x/sync minor upgrades into the module, and those are
shared with production code.

One commit rather than three, against the usual grain. The vendor tree is
coupled across all three parts (jsconsumer vendors only because part 3
imports it, nats-server only because part 2 does), so splitting would
leave intermediate commits failing `go mod tidy -diff` — a bisect landing
on a red commit costs more than this message being long.

./..., go test -race ./..., golangci-lint (0 issues) — all clean.

**PR-0 committed** on `nodo/cor-1254-pr0-jsconsumer-plumbing` (`5df2828`), checkpoint trailer attached by the hook. Full gate clean: build, vet, `go mod tidy -diff`, `git diff --check`, `gofmt -s`, `go test ./...`, `go test -race ./...`, golangci-lint 0 issues.

**What landed** — 4 non-vendor files, the rest is vendor:

- **go-nuts → `832d765`.** The old pin predated trail #13 by two days; the vendored tree had no `jsconsumer` at all.
- **`internal/natstest`** — embedded JetStream broker exposing *both* handles on one server, so a migration can be measured (characterise the legacy loop, then show the new one reproduces it) rather than asserted against two different fakes.
- **`internal/timingcontract`** — timing as data, checked by `jsconsumer.Schedule`, plus the before/after table renderer. Pure: no `testing` import, no clock.

**One measurement worth having now.** `REDACTED` confirms against a real broker the fact the worker exception rests on: requested AckWait 5s with `BackOff[0]` 200ms → **stored AckWait 200ms**. The class rule you ratified is now pinned by a test rather than by my reading. And the renderer already validates Shape A for loop 2 — give-up on delivery 8 at `t+3m30s` both before and after, capture reserve at `t+4m0s`, via the real validator.

**Two calls I made** — flag if you disagree:

input.title: PR-0: go-nuts 832d765, an embedded-broker harness, and a timing-contract helper
input.body:
Shared plumbing for Track D (COR-1254, implementing COR-1009 ph. 5). **No consumer, no durable, no fleet file.** Every later loop PR bases on this so each one carries a migration and nothing else.

Four non-vendor files. The rest of the diff is `vendor/`.

## Why a PR-0 at all

Three changes that all twelve loop PRs would otherwise each carry, and conflict on:

**1. go-nuts `v0.9.1-0.20260811083507` → `v0.9.1-0.20260813130528-832d765dac1b`.** The old pin predates trail #13 by two days, so the vendored tree had no `jsconsumer` package at all and `natsmsg` was missing `KeepInProgress`'s tick cap and the DLQ publisher's header policy. Nothing here imports `jsconsumer` yet — it vendors because `internal/timingcontract` does.

**2. `internal/natstest` — an embedded JetStream nats-server for tests.** mirror-pipeline has had *zero* broker-level coverage: every consume-loop test drives interface fakes (`ackableMsg`, `fanoutengine.AckableMsg`, `messageFetcher`) that encode the same model as the code, so they agree with it exactly when it is wrong. That is the gap COR-1009 names as a gate for the loop ports, and the one go-nuts closed for itself with `internal/brokersemantics` after every P1 in the A1 review cycle turned out to be a model error rather than a coding one.

It exposes **both** handles on one broker — `LegacyJetStream` for the loops as they are today, `JetStream` for a migrated one — so a migration can be *measured* rather than asserted: characterise the legacy loop, then show the new one reproduces it. Two assertions written against two different fakes are not evidence of anything.

**3. `internal/timingcontract` — a consumer's redelivery timing as data**, checked by go-nuts' exported `jsconsumer.Schedule` rather than by hand, plus the renderer for the before/after table every migration trail carries. ENT-1535 was a consumer whose real envelope was 34h22m against a config advertising 17h45m; duplicated timing arithmetic is how that happens, so nothing is restated here. Two loops in this repo — `cmd/worker` and the meta-fanout lifecycle fan — carry neither a server ladder nor a `Retry`, so `jsconsumer.Start`'s own schedule check never runs for them, which is exactly why it has to be reachable from a test.

Pure by construction: no `testing` import, no NATS connection, no clock, so it carries none of `natstest`'s production-import hazard.

## The measurement worth reading

`REDACTED` pins, against a real broker, the fact `cmd/worker`'s client-ladder exception rests on — now recorded on COR-1254 as a class rule rather than a worker quirk:

```
nats-server 2.14.4: requested AckWait 5s with BackOff[0] 200ms, stored AckWait 200ms
```

A durable given a `BackOff` ladder does not keep its requested `AckWait`; the server stores `BackOff[0]` in its place. So "own the ladder server-side" and "keep this AckWait" are one knob, not two — and combined with `natsmsg.KeepInProgress`'s ~5×AckWait cap, a 30s first rung would collapse the worker's extension budget from 75m to 2m30s and redeliver 30-minute clones mid-run. The fixture uses **growing** rungs deliberately: on a flat ladder the assertion passes whether the normalization happens or not.

The other two tests: `TestVersionAttribution` keeps a broker-semantic failure attributable to a server version, and `TestNoProductionImport` keeps the embedded server out of shipped binaries — guarding itself against passing vacuously by pinning that the walk actually reached a known consume loop, rather than trusting that a walk which found nothing means nothing is wrong.

## Loop 2's ladder, validated ahead of time

`internal/timingcontract`'s renderer, run over the webhook-forwarder Shape A shape approved for loop 2. Both contracts pass `jsconsumer.Schedule.Validate()`; the envelope is preserved byte-for-byte:

```
| delivery | before (client Nak) | after (server ladder) |
|---:|---|---|
| 1 | t+0s | t+0s |
| 2 | t+30s | t+30s |
| 3 | t+1m0s | t+1m0s |
| 4 | t+1m30s | t+1m30s |
| 5 | t+2m0s | t+2m0s |
| 6 | t+2m30s | t+2m30s |
| 7 | t+3m0s | t+3m0s |
| 8 | t+3m30s — give up | t+3m30s — give up |
| 9 |  | t+4m0s — capture reserve |
```

The blank 9th cell for the before contract is deliberate: the two schedules have different caps, and a `0s` there would read as an instant retry.

## Two judgment calls

**nats-server pinned to 2.14.4, not the 2.14.3 go-nuts resolves.** The harness exists to attribute semantics to the server that actually runs, and fleet runs 2.14.4 (`apps/nats/base/helmrelease.yaml`). It is a test-only dependency, so no shipped binary changes — **but** it pulls `x/sys`, `x/text` and `x/sync` minor upgrades into the module, and those are shared with production code. Flagging rather than burying: a test-only dep moving shared libraries is worth a reviewer's eye.

**One commit rather than three, against the usual grain.** The vendor tree is coupled across all three parts (`jsconsumer` vendors only because part 3 imports it, `nats-server` only because part 2 does), so splitting would leave intermediate commits failing `go mod tidy -diff`. A bisect landing on a red commit costs more than one long commit message.

## Per-PR template

Both items from the binding template are **N/A for this PR, stated rather than skipped**:

- **(a) stored-vs-rendered `nats consumer info -j` diff** — this PR touches no durable and creates no consumer. The first PR that needs it is loop 1 (`meta-fanout-lifecycle`, one durable per cell). Note for planning: no MCP tool exposes consumer *config* — `nats_stream_consumers` returns runtime state only (ack floor, pending, redelivered, waiting) — so the snapshot has to come from someone with cluster credentials, per PR, until that gap is closed.
- **(b) monitor/runbook text delta** — no give-up semantics change here, so there is nothing for a responder to re-learn. Loop 2 is where that starts (capture-then-Ack silences the `MAX_DELIVERIES`/`MSG_TERMINATED` advisory backstops on the normal path).

## Gate

`go build ./...`, `go vet ./...`, `go mod tidy -diff`, `git diff --check`, `gofmt -l -s`, `go test ./...`, `go test -race ./...`, `mise run lint` (golangci-lint 2.11.2 — 0 issues). All clean.

## Reviewing this

The vendor diff is ~205k lines and carries no information; read the four files under `internal/natstest/` and `internal/timingcontract/`, plus `go.mod`. The two questions worth pressing on are whether the 2.14.4 pin is right and whether `TestNoProductionImport`'s self-guards are strong enough to be worth having.

# natsctl — thin launcher that runs the stock `nats` CLI in-cluster, on-demand,
# under the least-privilege `natsctl` mTLS identity. It derives a one-off Job
# from the suspended `natsctl` CronJob (fleet apps/natsctl — the GitOps-pinned
# nats-box image + internal-tls cert + NATS env), injects your `nats` arguments,

# (apps/nats) is granted JetStream read verbs (STREAM/CONSUMER INFO/LIST/NAMES,
# MSG.GET, DIRECT.GET, ephemeral ordered consumers) plus STREAM.PURGE and
# per-message STREAM.MSG.DELETE on the enumerated dead-letter capture streams
# (listed under NOTES in --help) so a triaged DLQ can
# be drained or pruned without the break-glass admin pod. Every OTHER mutating
# verb — purge/rmm of any other stream, rm, edit, pub — fails with a NATS

content.text: Two durables carry an **orphaned server ladder** their code doesn't know about. Correcting my own trail claim first.

input.body:
**Correction to this trail's body, from the loop-1 pre-flight: the "before" column of the timing table is not the live before-state for webhook-forwarder.** The code in this PR is unaffected — the renderer and its fixtures are fine, and the gate still stands. What is wrong is the framing "the envelope is preserved byte-for-byte", which described a fixture I built from the app's constants rather than from the durable.

Measured just now via `natsctl` on `eks-staging-us-west-2` (`consumer info webhooks_github_v1 <durable> --json`):

| durable | code declares | server actually stores | real envelope |
|---|---|---|---|
| `webhook-forwarder` | no `BackOff`, client `NakWithDelay(30s)` | `backoff: [30s, 2m, 10m, 1h, 4h, 12h, 24h]` | **41h12m30s** |
| `fanout-us-west-2` | no `BackOff`, client `NakWithDelay(30s)` | same 7 rungs | **41h12m30s** |
| `core-fanout` | no `BackOff` | absent | 3m30s — code and server agree |
| `meta-fanout` | no `BackOff` | absent | 3m30s — agree |
| `trails-fanout-push` | no `BackOff` | absent | 3m30s — agree |
| `trails-fanout-pull-request` | no `BackOff` | absent | 3m30s — agree |
| `meta-fanout-lifecycle` (all 3 staging cells) | no `BackOff` | absent | 3m30s — agree |

Two durables are carrying a **live ENT-1535**: mixed ownership, with the client's flat 30s Nak and a server ladder nobody's code declares. Because the requested delay equals `BackOff[0]`, the stretch term is zero on the first rung and the redeliveries then follow the SERVER ladder exactly — so the effective envelope is 41h12m30s against a code comment (`cmd/webhook-forwarder/forwarder.go:48-52`) that reads "No `nats.BackOff` is set, so this is a free choice — not clamped to a schedule."

The mechanism is visible in the code that disclaims it: `consumerMaxDeliver`'s comment notes "dropping `nats.BackOff` is tolerated (BackOff is not part of that comparison)". It is tolerated by `checkConfig`, which is exactly why the ladder outlived its removal from the source — legacy `PullSubscribe` binds to the existing durable and never updates it. The other four durables never had a ladder, so they never acquired an orphan.

Consequences, none of which change this PR:

1. **Loop 2 is no longer an envelope-preserving migration.** A declared flat 30s ladder would take the real give-up from 41h12m30s to 3m30s — a fix, but a ~700× behaviour change that needs its own decision, not a table claiming parity. A transient entire-web outage that today rides out on the 4h/12h/24h rungs would instead dead-letter in under four minutes, so DLQ volume and replay load both move. The entire-search precedent (`[5m, 5m, 5m, 12m, 15m]`, ~42m) looks like the better shape to reason from than either extreme.
2. **`fanout-<region>` inherits the same correction**, and it is loop 9 — the highest-traffic consumer, and the one adopting `Retry` while keeping its fetch loop.
3. **A stalled delivery on either durable can pin the ack floor for up to 41 hours today.** Within `webhooks_github_v1`'s 96h maxAge, so capture is still reached — but that is the stall class the ack-floor monitor pages on, and it is live right now.
4. **Prod is unverified.** `natsctl` against the four prod cells needs privileges my kube role does not have (`jobs.batch is forbidden` in the `natsctl` namespace). Same code history, so the same orphan is likely, but "likely" is not a snapshot.

Separate, smaller finding from the same sweep: **every** durable inspected carries `max_ack_pending: 65536`, which is not the server's 1000 default and not a tuned value — nats.go's legacy pull path copies its own client-side subscription-channel capacity (`js.go:1879-1880`, `cfg.MaxAckPending = cap(ch)`, default 65536) into the server config. `jsconsumer` leaving `MaxAckPending` at zero would silently rewrite every migrated durable to 1000. Harmless in effect for a serial consumer buffering one message, but it must be an explicit decision per loop rather than a side effect.

A delivery that keeps failing (entire-web 5xx, network error) holds the `webhooks_github_v1` **ack floor for up to 41 hours**. That stream is interest-retention with seven consumers, and a pinned floor is the ENT-1535/Aug 5–6 shape: the stall signal cannot distinguish one pinned message from a throughput collapse.

It is a **stall, not a loss**: 41h12m30s < the stream's 96h `maxAge`, so the delivery still reaches DLQ capture on delivery 8.

**Second finding — nothing observes this today.** The only per-consumer monitor on this stream (`monitor_ingest_consumer_backlog.tf`) fires on `num_pending + num_ack_pending > 5000` sustained over 20m — a *volume* signal, sized for the 2026-06-01 orphaned-durable starvation. A single message pinning the floor for 41h leaves `num_ack_pending` at 1 and never trips it. Unlike `repo_refs_v1`, `webhooks_github_v1` has **no ack-floor-age monitor at all**, so this behaviour is not merely undocumented — it is unmeasured.

## Proposed work

1. **Decide the intended envelope.** Options span 3m30s (a declared flat 30s ladder), ~42m (the entire-search shape `[5m, 5m, 5m, 12m, 15m]`), and ~4h (bounded but patient). The real question is how long an entire-web outage should be absorbed automatically versus dead-lettered for manual replay — `webhooks_github_dlq` retains 7 days in prod, and replay is a manual `mirrorctl` operation.
2. **Make it declared, not inherited.** Whichever envelope is chosen, it has to be written where the code says it is. Reconciling an existing durable's `BackOff` needs `CreateOrUpdateConsumer` (the modern client) — which is precisely what the Track D migration of these two loops does, so the fix and the migration can be the same change if the timing suits.
3. **Close the observability gap** — an ack-floor-age monitor on `webhooks_github_v1`, sized under whatever envelope is chosen.

## Relationship to Track D

Found by COR-1254's pre-flight and it changes that plan (loop 2 and loop 9 are no longer envelope-preserving migrations — see the correction on mirror-pipeline trail #100), but it is **not** created by the migration and should not wait on it. The migration is the natural vehicle for item 2; items 1 and 3 stand on their own.

Evidence: raw `consumer info` JSON for all seven durables across seven cells captured during the pre-flight; mirror-pipeline trail #100 carries the summary.

When I opened trail #100 I wrote in its description that loop 2's migration "preserves the envelope byte-for-byte", with a table showing 3m30s before and after. **That was wrong** — I'd built the table from the app's Go constants, before I'd looked at the actual durable. The durable says 41 hours.

So: **open trail #100, paste the contents of `trail-100-correction.md` as a comment.** That's the whole ask. It matters because anyone reviewing that trail right now reads a claim I know to be false.

If you'd rather not paste, reconnecting the entire MCP connector would let me post it directly — either way works.

## (2) The loop-2 ladder decision, with the context

**What the ladder is.** `webhook-forwarder` POSTs each GitHub webhook to entire-web. On a 5xx or network error the delivery is retried on a schedule. When the schedule runs out, the webhook is captured to `webhooks_github_dlq` and replayed **manually** via `mirrorctl`. So the ladder length is exactly: *how long an entire-web outage gets absorbed automatically before it becomes human work.*

**Today, measured:** 41h12m30s. An entire-web outage of up to ~41 hours is ridden out with nobody touching anything. Nothing was designed that way — it's leftover config.

**What I originally proposed** (flat 30s ×8 → 3m30s) I now think is wrong. A routine entire-web deploy or restart takes longer than 3½ minutes, so every webhook arriving during one would dead-letter. You'd trade an invisible 41-hour stall for a DLQ that fills on ordinary deploys and needs manual replay each time.

**The constraint I went looking for doesn't exist.** I expected an ack-floor monitor to bound this. There isn't one: the only per-consumer monitor on `webhooks_github_v1` fires on `num_pending + num_ack_pending > 5000` over 20m — a volume signal sized for the 2026-06-01 orphaned-durable case. One message pinning the floor for 41h keeps `num_ack_pending` at 1 and never trips it. So the current behaviour isn't just undocumented, it's unmeasured — which is why COR-1270 carries an observability item.

**So the decision is a judgement, and these are the numbers for it:**

| envelope | absorbs an outage of | floor pinned up to | manual replay when |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3m30s (flat 30s) | 3½ min | 3½ min | any deploy-length blip |
| ~42m (entire-search shape) | 40 min | 42 min | outage > 40 min |
| ~4h (e.g. `[30s,2m,10m,30m,1h,2h]`) | 4 hours | 4 hours | genuine multi-hour outage |
| 41h (today) | 41 hours | **41 hours** | almost never |

`webhooks_github_dlq` keeps 7 days in prod, so dead-lettering isn't lossy — it's a queue of manual work.

**My recommendation: the ~42m shape.** It matches the precedent Track A already set, absorbs every ordinary entire-web deploy, and caps the invisible-stall exposure at 42 minutes instead of 41 hours. If you'd rather not create replay work during longer incidents, the ~4h shape is the defensible alternative — but I'd pair it with the ack-floor monitor landing first, since 4 hours of unobserved pinning is a lot.

You don't need to settle this to unblock me: **loop 1 is clean and fully pre-flighted across all seven cells.** Want me to start it while you think about loop 2?

input.title: PR-0: go-nuts 832d765, an embedded-broker harness, and a timing-contract helper
input.body:
Shared plumbing for Track D (COR-1254, implementing COR-1009 ph. 5). **No consumer, no durable, no fleet file.** Every later loop PR bases on this so each one carries a migration and nothing else.

Four non-vendor files. The rest of the diff is `vendor/`.

## Why a PR-0 at all

Three changes that all twelve loop PRs would otherwise each carry, and conflict on:

**1. go-nuts `v0.9.1-0.20260811083507` → `v0.9.1-0.20260813130528-832d765dac1b`.** The old pin predates trail #13 by two days, so the vendored tree had no `jsconsumer` package at all and `natsmsg` was missing `KeepInProgress`'s tick cap and the DLQ publisher's header policy. Nothing here imports `jsconsumer` yet — it vendors because `internal/timingcontract` does.

**2. `internal/natstest` — an embedded JetStream nats-server for tests.** mirror-pipeline has had *zero* broker-level coverage: every consume-loop test drives interface fakes (`ackableMsg`, `fanoutengine.AckableMsg`, `messageFetcher`) that encode the same model as the code, so they agree with it exactly when it is wrong. That is the gap COR-1009 names as a gate for the loop ports, and the one go-nuts closed for itself with `internal/brokersemantics` after every P1 in the A1 review cycle turned out to be a model error rather than a coding one.

It exposes **both** handles on one broker — `LegacyJetStream` for the loops as they are today, `JetStream` for a migrated one — so a migration can be *measured* rather than asserted: characterise the legacy loop, then show the new one reproduces it. Two assertions written against two different fakes are not evidence of anything.

**3. `internal/timingcontract` — a consumer's redelivery timing as data**, checked by go-nuts' exported `jsconsumer.Schedule` rather than by hand, plus the renderer for the before/after table every migration trail carries. ENT-1535 was a consumer whose real envelope was 34h22m against a config advertising 17h45m; duplicated timing arithmetic is how that happens, so nothing is restated here. Two loops in this repo — `cmd/worker` and the meta-fanout lifecycle fan — carry neither a server ladder nor a `Retry`, so `jsconsumer.Start`'s own schedule check never runs for them, which is exactly why it has to be reachable from a test.

Pure by construction: no `testing` import, no NATS connection, no clock, so it carries none of `natstest`'s production-import hazard.

## This PR already found something

Building the second commit's fixture from the *durable* rather than from the app's constants surfaced a live defect, now filed as **COR-1270**. Measured via `natsctl -- consumer info webhooks_github_v1 <durable> --json` on prod us-east-2 and staging us-west-2 alike:

| durable | code declares | server actually stores | real envelope |
|---|---|---|---|
| `webhook-forwarder` | no `BackOff`, client `NakWithDelay(30s)` | `[30s, 2m, 10m, 1h, 4h, 12h, 24h]` | **41h12m30s** |
| `fanout-us-east-2` | no `BackOff`, client `NakWithDelay(30s)` | same 7 rungs | **41h12m30s** |
| `core-fanout`, `meta-fanout`, `trails-fanout-push`, `trails-fanout-pull-request` | no `BackOff` | absent | 3m30s — code and server agree |

Two consumers run a ladder no source file declares, alongside the app's own client-side Nak — mixed ownership, i.e. a live ENT-1535, in production. Because the requested delay equals `BackOff[0]`, the stretch term is zero on the first rung and redeliveries follow the SERVER ladder exactly, so the real give-up is 41 hours against a comment (`forwarder.go:48-52`) reading "No `nats.BackOff` is set, so this is a free choice — not clamped to a schedule."

The mechanism is admitted two lines up in the same file: *"dropping `nats.BackOff` is tolerated (BackOff is not part of that comparison)"*. It is tolerated by `checkConfig`, which is why the ladder outlived its deletion from the source — legacy `PullSubscribe` binds and never updates. The four durables that never had a ladder never acquired an orphan.

This predates the migration and does not block this PR; COR-1270 owns the fix and the missing ack-floor observability.

## The measurement worth reading

`natstest.REDACTED` pins, against a real broker, the fact `cmd/worker`'s client-ladder exception rests on — recorded on COR-1254 as a class rule rather than a worker quirk:

```
nats-server 2.14.4: requested AckWait 5s with BackOff[0] 200ms, stored AckWait 200ms
```

A durable given a `BackOff` ladder does not keep its requested `AckWait`; the server stores `BackOff[0]` in its place. So "own the ladder server-side" and "keep this AckWait" are one knob, not two — and with `natsmsg.KeepInProgress`'s ~5×AckWait cap, a 30s first rung would collapse the worker's extension budget from 75m to 2m30s and redeliver 30-minute clones mid-run. The fixture uses **growing** rungs deliberately: on a flat ladder the assertion passes whether the normalization happens or not.

The other two: `TestVersionAttribution` keeps a broker-semantic failure attributable to a server version, and `TestNoProductionImport` keeps the embedded server out of shipped binaries — guarding itself against a vacuous pass by pinning that the walk actually reached a known consume loop.

## Loop 2's ladder, validated ahead of time

Generated by `internal/timingcontract` from the measured "before" and the decided ~40m "after", both coherent under `jsconsumer.Schedule.Validate()`:

```
| delivery | before (measured, orphaned ladder) | after (declared ~40m ladder) |
|---:|---|---|
| 1 | t+0s | t+0s |
| 2 | t+30s | t+30s |
| 3 | t+2m30s | t+2m30s |
| 4 | t+12m30s | t+7m30s |
| 5 | t+1h12m30s | t+19m30s |
| 6 | t+5h12m30s | t+39m30s — give up |
| 7 | t+17h12m30s | t+59m30s — capture reserve |
| 8 | t+41h12m30s — give up |  |
```

~40m is patient enough to absorb an ordinary entire-web deploy without manufacturing manual DLQ replay, and short enough that a pinned ack floor is a 40-minute exposure rather than a 41-hour one. The rung values are a proposal for loop 2's own review; what the test pins is that they are coherent and hit the decided envelope. `AckWait` deliberately stays 30s by keeping `BackOff[0]` at 30s — with a server ladder those are one knob, so entire-search's 5m first rung would also slow post-crash redelivery 10×, and this handler is a single fast POST behind a one-message prefetch.

The "before" envelope is asserted too, so the snapshot cannot rot silently: if someone reconciles that durable, the test goes red and names the date the measurement was taken.

## Two judgment calls

**nats-server pinned to 2.14.4, not the 2.14.3 go-nuts resolves.** The harness exists to attribute semantics to the server that actually runs, and fleet runs 2.14.4 (`apps/nats/base/helmrelease.yaml`). Test-only, so no shipped binary changes — **but** it pulls `x/sys`, `x/text` and `x/sync` minor upgrades into the module, and those are shared with production code.

**One commit for the plumbing rather than three.** The vendor tree is coupled across all three parts (`jsconsumer` vendors only because part 3 imports it, `nats-server` only because part 2 does), so splitting would leave intermediate commits failing `go mod tidy -diff`. The second commit is the fixture correction above, kept separate because it is a finding rather than plumbing.

## Per-PR template

- **(a) stored-vs-rendered `nats consumer info -j` diff** — N/A: this PR touches no durable and creates no consumer. Loop 1's pre-flight is nevertheless complete, and clean: `meta-fanout-lifecycle` is identical across all seven cells (4 prod + 3 staging) — `ackWait 30s`, `maxDeliver 8`, no `backoff`, no `inactiveThreshold`, `maxAckPending 65536`, `deliverPolicy all`, `replayPolicy instant`, `ackPolicy explicit`, `maxWaiting 512`, `numReplicas 0`. The one field a migration would move unintentionally is `max_ack_pending`: **every** durable in every cell carries 65536, which is neither the server's 1000 default nor a tuned value — nats.go's legacy pull path copies its own subscription-channel capacity into the server config (`js.go:1879-1880`, `cfg.MaxAckPending = cap(ch)`). Leaving `MaxAckPending` at zero would silently rewrite it to 1000, so each loop states it explicitly.
- **(b) monitor/runbook text delta** — N/A: no give-up semantics change here. Loop 2 is where that starts (capture-then-Ack silences the `MAX_DELIVERIES`/`MSG_TERMINATED` advisory backstops on the normal path), and COR-1270 carries the ack-floor monitor that stream lacks entirely.

## Gate

`go build ./...`, `go vet ./...`, `go mod tidy -diff`, `git diff --check`, `gofmt -l -s`, `go test ./...`, `go test -race ./...`, `mise run lint` (golangci-lint 2.11.2 — 0 issues). All clean.

## Reviewing this

The vendor diff is ~205k lines and carries no information; read the four files under `internal/natstest/` and `internal/timingcontract/`, plus `go.mod`. Worth pressing on: whether the 2.14.4 pin is right, and whether `TestNoProductionImport`'s self-guards earn their keep.

```
• Request changes on draft PR #245 (ba09d45…ccd8751). Two findings:
```
